title: The Eldest Son's Share
scenario: When their father died in Lahore, brothers Imran and Faisal Qureshi learned that the will, drawn up under local custom, gives sisters Nadia and Rubina smaller shares than Islamic inheritance rules would allow. Imran, a school principal and the executor, knows the sisters never questioned it. Faisal says changing it would force the sale of the family orchard, which sustains their mother. Imran has to file the paperwork this week and decide whether to raise the discrepancy.
options: File the will as written, respecting the father's wishes and the orchard's role in supporting their mother.
Tell the sisters about the discrepancy and offer to correct the distribution, even if the orchard must be partly sold.
Propose that the brothers pay the sisters the difference over several years, preserving the orchard while correcting the shortfall.
tension: fidelity to the will vs. fairness

title: A Debt Bigger Than the House
scenario: Beatriz Alencar, 35, a dentist in Recife, inherits her late father's small apartment, but also discovers he owed a large sum to a loan shark-like lender in the neighbourhood. Brazilian law would let her renounce the inheritance and avoid the debt, but the apartment houses her aunt, who has nowhere else to go. Her brother urges her to renounce and walk away. The lender has begun phoning the aunt. Beatriz must decide before the legal deadline.
options: Renounce the inheritance to protect her own finances and help the aunt find housing by other means.
Accept the apartment and negotiate with the lender, taking on risk to keep her aunt in her home.
Accept it and sell, paying the debt and splitting any remainder with her brother, forcing the aunt to move.

title: The Dowry Land
scenario: In Rajasthan, Sunita Meena's father promised her brother the family's farmland while giving Sunita only a wedding. After his death, local panchayat norms favour the brother, but Sunita's marriage has ended and she has two children and no income. Her brother Mohan is struggling with crop debt himself. Sunita can petition for a legal share under national law, which would split the land too thinly to farm. She must decide whether to file.
options: File for her legal share, asserting equal rights as a child of the deceased and securing her children's future.
Forgo the claim in return for a negotiated yearly payment from the harvest, preserving the farm and relations.
Withdraw and seek wage work in the city, keeping peace with her brother and village while accepting reduced security.

title: Granddad's Painting
scenario: Three cousins in Edinburgh, Callum, Isla and Rory Munro, discover that a landscape painting hanging in their late grandfather's house is worth far more than the house itself. The will leaves everything to be divided equally, but Rory, a struggling artist, has cared for the grandfather for years and says he was promised the painting. Callum wants to sell and split the proceeds. Isla, the executor, must decide how to carry out the estate at tomorrow's meeting.
options: Sell the painting and divide the proceeds equally, following the written will rather than uncertain verbal promises.
Give Rory the painting as an acknowledgement of his care, even though this reduces the cousins' shares.
Sell it, but allocate Rory an additional payment from the estate for caregiving, balancing fairness with recognition.
tension: compensation for care vs. equal shares

title: Burying Him Where?
scenario: Old Mr. Adeyemi Balogun, a Nigerian trader, died in London, leaving a will that directs his estate be shared among his Yoruba family and a second household he kept quiet for thirty years in Ibadan. His London-born daughter Folake, the executor, discovers a second wife and a teenage son. Her mother, still alive, begs her to ignore the second family. Folake can contest their claim on technical grounds or follow the will. She must decide how to proceed before probate.
options: Honour the will and include the second family, accepting her mother's anguish and the exposure of her father's secret.
Contest the second family's claim on a technicality, protecting her mother's feelings and the primary household's finances.
Share the secret with her mother first and let her decide, even if that delays probate and deepens family conflict.
tension: honouring the dead vs. protecting the living

title: The Taro Patch Question
scenario: On the island of Savai'i, Lupe Aiono holds customary rights to a taro plantation that her late father used. Her brother Tevita, who lives in Sydney, sends money each year and wants the land registered in his name for investment. Village custom would give the cultivating child priority, but Tevita says the money is what kept the land during drought. Lupe, 40, must tell the village council whether she accepts his claim.
options: Reject Tevita's claim and assert her cultivation rights, resting on village custom and her daily labour.
Accept shared registration, recognising his financial contributions and avoiding a family rupture.
Propose a lease arrangement in which she farms and pays Tevita a small share, trying to separate use from ownership.

title: The Letter in the Safe
scenario: After the death of her father in Warsaw, accountant Zofia Nowicka finds a sealed letter in his safe addressed to her brother Marek. It apologises for leaving Marek out of the will after a quarrel and asks Zofia to share her inheritance equally. The letter has no legal force. Zofia was helped through years of hardship by their father and lives modestly; Marek is wealthy but has not spoken to the family in a decade. Zofia must decide what to do with the letter.
options: Give Marek the letter and split the inheritance equally, treating their father's wish as morally binding.
Give Marek the letter but keep the inheritance, treating the request as unenforceable and the estrangement as Marek's choice.
Destroy the letter and say nothing, arguing that the will reflects the father's final legal choice and avoiding conflict.
tension: honouring last wishes vs. legal will

title: A Kingdom of Three Chairs
scenario: Ibrahim Traore is the youngest son of a Malian cloth merchant whose business in Bamako was meant to pass to the eldest, Moussa. Moussa has left for France and shows no interest. The middle brother, Seydou, has run the business for five years without ownership. A family elder says tradition requires Moussa's consent for any change. Ibrahim, a lawyer, is asked to propose a settlement at the family council this Friday.
options: Propose that ownership pass to Seydou, who works the business, and seek Moussa's consent through phone calls from the elders.
Uphold the tradition that Moussa holds title and propose Seydou be paid a salary, preserving the family order.
Propose dividing the business into three equal shares, ignoring seniority and trying to treat each brother as equal.

title: What the Widow Never Asked For
scenario: Eleni Papadakis, 61, in Thessaloniki, is told by her late husband's family that in their tradition the widow does not inherit the farmhouse, which goes to the male line. Eleni helped renovate it and lives there. The nephew who would inherit has offered to let her stay for life. A lawyer says Greek law protects her share, but contesting would split a village already divided by feuds. Eleni must decide whether to accept the nephew's offer or pursue her claim.
options: Accept the nephew's life-tenancy offer, valuing peace and the continuity of her home over a formal claim.
Pursue her legal share, defending her rights as a widow and securing her place against future changes of heart.
Accept the offer but insist on a written, notarised agreement to protect against later disputes.

title: Cattle for the Younger Brother
scenario: In Kajiado, Kenya, Joseph Lenkai inherits a herd of cattle from his father, which in Maasai custom would be shared with extended kin and used for his younger brother Saruni's bride price. Joseph has a diploma in business and wants to sell half to start a transport business in Nairobi. Saruni, 20, cannot marry without the cattle. Elders are watching. Joseph must say at the clan gathering how he will use the herd.
options: Give Saruni the cattle he needs for the bride price, honouring the clan's expectations and his brother's future.
Sell half and invest in the business, justifying it as a way to support the whole family in the long run.
Lend Saruni the cattle and promise repayment from business profits, risking delay and disputes if the plan fails.

title: Mother's Will, Brother's Gambling
scenario: Priscilla Tan, a 53-year-old nurse in Kuala Lumpur, learns that her mother wants to leave the family terrace house equally to her and her brother Desmond. Desmond has gambling debts and has sold family items before. Their mother, 84 and forgetful, trusts him. Priscilla has helped pay her mother's bills for years. She can ask the mother to set up a trust or simply keep quiet. She has an appointment with the mother's lawyer on Monday.
options: Ask the lawyer to structure a trust that limits Desmond's access, risking her mother's feelings and a break with her brother.
Keep quiet and let the will stand, trusting that her mother knows her son and that interference would be a betrayal.
Talk privately with Desmond first and ask him to agree to a managed arrangement, risking denial or retaliation.

title: The Stepmother's Case
scenario: Rolf Lindqvist, a Swedish architect in Gothenburg, is told by his late father's second wife, Birgit, that she assumed she would remain in the lakeside cottage for life. The cottage was Rolf's grandmother's, and Rolf's father left it to Rolf. Birgit has few savings and poor health. Rolf's sister wants to sell it and divide the proceeds. Rolf must tell Birgit by the end of the month whether she can stay.
options: Let Birgit stay for life without rent, treating her years with his father as a claim of moral weight.
Sell the cottage with his sister as the will implies and help Birgit find housing with a modest contribution.
Allow her to stay for a fixed period, such as two years, then sell, trying to give her time without indefinite sacrifice.

title: A Palace Without Heirs
scenario: Chao Phraya Suwannarat's grandson, Nattapong, 28, a Bangkok software engineer, inherits a decaying teak mansion in Ayutthaya with a spirit house that relatives believe protects the family's fortune. Maintenance costs are huge, and a developer offers to buy it for a hotel. Elderly aunts fear selling would anger ancestors and bring misfortune. Nattapong does not share their beliefs but loves them. The developer wants an answer by the end of the week.
options: Sell to the developer and fund care for the aunts, valuing present people over speculative ancestral displeasure.
Keep the mansion and fund repairs through loans, honouring the aunts' beliefs and the family's heritage at financial risk.
Sell but require the developer to preserve the spirit house and give the aunts lifetime visiting rights.

title: Uncle's Land Without a Deed
scenario: Farhan Mirza, 31, a surveyor in Kabul, discovers that his late uncle's orchard was never formally registered, though Farhan's cousins have all assumed it belongs to them. In truth, Farhan's father bought half of it decades ago on a handshake. Farhan could register his claim, which a court would probably accept, but the cousins, who are poorer, depend on the full orchard. A village mediator offers to hear both sides next week.
options: Register his father's claimed half and defend it, asserting a legitimate property right.
Waive the claim, honouring the shared assumption and the cousins' need, even though it reduces his own inheritance.
Take the dispute to the mediator and accept whatever split emerges, hoping for communal legitimacy at the cost of uncertainty.

title: The Tango Studio
scenario: After her mother's death in Montevideo, dancer Valentina Rocha inherits half of a tango studio, while her estranged uncle Gonzalo inherits the other half. Gonzalo wants to sell to a chain gym, while Valentina's students and old teachers rely on the space. Gonzalo is unemployed and has two sons in school. Valentina can buy him out only by borrowing heavily. She must give him an answer before the offer from the chain expires.
options: Borrow heavily to buy out Gonzalo, protecting the community's studio at serious personal financial risk.
Agree to sell, giving Gonzalo his share of the proceeds, accepting the loss of the studio to protect her finances and family fairness.
Offer Gonzalo a rental income from the studio over time, trying to meet his needs without selling, with uncertain profitability.

title: Names on the Ancestral Shrine
scenario: Truong Thi Mai, 46, in Hue, finds that her father's will leaves the family altar and ancestral land to her brother, as is common, while she cares for their mother daily. The brother lives abroad and rarely visits. A relative says that daughters give up claims once married. Mai is now divorced, supports her teenage son, and could use the land's rent. She must tell the family at the death anniversary gathering what she intends.
options: Accept the traditional arrangement and say nothing, preserving ritual order and peace at the gathering.
Ask for a share of the rent as compensation for caring for their mother, framing it as fairness rather than rights.
Assert a legal claim to an equal share of the land, grounding it in national law and her contributions.

title: Grandma's Jewellery in Istanbul
scenario: Cem Arslan, 27, a pharmacist in Istanbul, finds that his late grandmother's jewellery, promised verbally to his cousin Defne at her wedding, is listed in the will as divided among all grandchildren. Defne is facing medical bills for her husband. The other cousins, who barely knew the grandmother, want to sell their shares. Cem holds the key to the safe and has been asked to distribute the items. He must decide how to proceed.
options: Follow the will and divide the jewellery equally, treating the written document as the clearest guide.
Give Defne her promised pieces, relying on the grandmother's stated wishes and her current need.
Convene all the cousins to decide together, risking disagreement but giving everyone a voice.

title: The Family Restaurant on Rue Victor
scenario: Amadou Diallo, 49, manages a Senegalese restaurant in Paris that his late uncle opened, with all relatives owning shares. Cousins in Dakar expect dividends that the restaurant, hit by rising rent, cannot pay. Amadou can sell the lease to a chain, ending his own job and those of four employees, or cut employees' hours to keep paying dividends. The shareholders meet next month. Amadou must decide which proposal to bring.
options: Propose selling the lease, paying shareholders fairly and accepting the loss of employees' jobs.
Propose reducing dividends sharply to protect employees, risking the anger of relatives who count on remittances.
Propose keeping dividends and cutting employee hours, honouring kin first despite harm to staff.

title: A Lawyer's Silence
scenario: Attorney Moira Gallagher in Dublin is asked by her client, Dermot O'Hara, 80, to draft a will leaving his farm to his son who stayed and worked it, and nothing to his daughter in America whom he considers disloyal. Moira suspects the daughter once sent money that saved the farm. Dermot has capacity and insists on privacy. Moira is not permitted to disclose, but she can ask questions. She must decide how to advise at the next appointment.
options: Draft the will as instructed and advise nothing further, respecting Dermot's autonomy and confidentiality.
Raise the possibility of the daughter's earlier help and urge him to reconsider, at risk of overstepping her role.
Suggest a modest legacy for the daughter as a protection against legal challenge, framing it as practical advice.
tension: client autonomy vs. fairness to third party

title: The Apprenticeship Fund
scenario: Ngozi Eze's late father in Onitsha left a modest fund meant for the education of his grandchildren. Ngozi, the executor, finds that her sister's twin boys are excellent students, while her brother's son has fallen behind and may need vocational training. The will says 'equally among grandchildren' without guidance on need or merit. The fund can cover either university tuition for the twins or training for the brother's son, but not all. She must decide on the terms of distribution.
options: Divide the fund equally in cash among all grandchildren, following the will literally and leaving families to decide use.
Direct the fund toward the twins' university fees, maximising the use of the fund on likelier long-term outcomes.
Direct the fund toward the brother's son's training, favouring the grandchild with the greatest present need.

title: An Inheritance for the Caregiver
scenario: Lakshmi Perera in Colombo works as a paid live-in caregiver for the elderly Mrs. Wijesinghe. Before her death, Mrs. Wijesinghe tells Lakshmi that she has changed her will to leave Lakshmi the seaside bungalow. Her children, who rarely visited, learn of this and accuse Lakshmi of manipulation. Lakshmi was surprised and did not request it. The family lawyer says the change may be valid. Lakshmi must decide whether to accept the bungalow if the will is upheld.
options: Accept the bungalow if the will is upheld, seeing it as a legitimate expression of Mrs. Wijesinghe's gratitude.
Decline the bungalow to remove suspicion and preserve her own reputation and the family's goodwill.
Accept and offer the children the right to buy it at a fair price, trying to answer both claims.

title: The Fishing Boat Quota
scenario: Magnus Jonsson, 58, an Icelandic skipper in Husavik, plans to pass his boat and fishing quota, a valuable asset, to his son Einar, who works in Reykjavik as a teacher and has no wish to fish. His daughter Sigrun fishes with him but, in the family's expectation, would not inherit. The quota is worth far more than Magnus's other assets. He needs to decide, before the season starts, how to name heirs.
options: Leave the boat and quota to Sigrun, who actually uses them, and compensate Einar with other assets.
Leave them to Einar as the son, who can lease them out, keeping with family expectation but denying Sigrun's work.
Leave the boat and quota jointly to both, risking disagreements about management and sale.

title: What the Monks Were Promised
scenario: Ven. Kyaw Min, a Burmese temple trustee in Mandalay, is approached by the children of a recently deceased donor. The donor had promised in life to give land to the monastery, but wrote nothing down. The children, struggling after the economic crash, ask the monastery to release them from the promise. The abbot is reluctant to appear grasping; some villagers insist a promise to the sangha cannot be broken. Kyaw Min must advise the abbot this evening.
options: Advise the abbot to accept the land if the children confirm the promise, upholding the donor's merit-making intent.
Advise releasing the children from the promise, recognising their hardship and avoiding a burden on grieving, struggling people.
Advise accepting a smaller portion of the land, trying to honour the promise partially while easing the children's burden.

title: Two Surnames, One House
scenario: Paloma Iglesias, a notary in Seville, handles the estate of an old man who left his house to his stepdaughter Rocio, the child he raised, while his biological son Andres from an earlier marriage seldom visited. Spanish forced-heirship rules give Andres a legal share. Rocio tells Paloma privately that Andres has been harassing her and that she cannot afford to pay him out. Paloma must decide how to explain the legal position at the signing.
options: Explain the law plainly to both and enforce Andres's legal share, treating her duty as one of neutral compliance.
Offer to help Rocio find a payment plan for Andres, using flexibility within the law to soften the burden on her.
Suggest Andres voluntarily waive his share in light of Rocio's care for the father, risking being seen as taking sides.

title: The Pension He Never Declared
scenario: Dang Quoc Huy, 34, a bookkeeper in Ho Chi Minh City, helps his deceased father's estate and notices that his father continued to receive a war-widow pension for his own mother years after she died. The money funded Huy's education and his siblings' needs. Reporting the error might require repayment of a large sum the family cannot afford. His siblings argue that their father already carried the consequences. Huy must decide whether to report it when filing the estate.
options: Report the error and propose repayment arrangements, treating honesty with the state as binding even at a cost to the family.
Leave the matter unmentioned, reasoning that the money was spent long ago and revealing it would only ruin the family.
Consult the pension office informally and ask about options without admitting details, trying to learn the risk before deciding.
tension: civic duty vs. loyalty to the dead
